questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define the term consumer surplus. (2 marks)

(ii) Suppose on arriving the market, only ice cream is available and free of charge. What quantity of ice cream will this individual consume to attain satiety and why? (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Consumer surplus** is **the difference between the maximum amount a consumer is willing to pay for a good (the total utility or benefit received, measured in money) and the amount he or she actually pays for it**. It is the extra satisfaction gained because the market price is lower than the value the consumer places on the units bought. For example, if a consumer would pay 1 500 FCFA for a plate of rice but the price is 1 000 FCFA, the consumer surplus is 500 FCFA. On a demand curve it is the area below the curve and above the price line.

**(ii) The consumer will consume 5 units of ice cream.**

First find the marginal utility (MU) of each unit, that is the change in total utility (TU) from one more unit:

| Units of ice cream | TU (Utils) | MU (Utils) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 90 | 90 |
| 2 | 150 | 60 |
| 3 | 180 | 30 |
| 4 | 200 | 20 |
| 5 | 200 | 0 |
| 6 | 180 | $-20$ |

- **Satiety** is the point of complete satisfaction, where **marginal utility is zero and total utility is at its maximum**. This happens at the 5th unit: TU stops rising (200 Utils) and MU = 0.
- Because ice cream is **free**, the price is zero, so the consumer pays nothing for each extra unit. A rational consumer therefore keeps consuming as long as MU is positive (extra satisfaction at no cost) and stops when MU reaches zero, at **5 units**.
- He will not take a 6th unit, because its MU is negative ($-20$ Utils): TU would fall from 200 to 180 Utils, which is disutility (the law of diminishing marginal utility).

questions.enonce_markdown: Determine the consumer's equilibrium given that all the goods are now available at the prices given above and that the consumer does not have any advantage of keeping money. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Condition for consumer equilibrium (equi-marginal principle).** A rational consumer maximises total utility when

$$
\frac{MU_{\text{ice cream}}}{P_{\text{ice cream}}} = \frac{MU_{\text{cake}}}{P_{\text{cake}}}
$$

and the whole budget is spent. Here the consumer gains nothing from keeping money, so all 5 000 FCFA is spent: $1\,000 \times Q_{\text{ice cream}} + 500 \times Q_{\text{cake}} = 5\,000$.

**Step 1: marginal utilities** (change in total utility from Table 1).

**Step 2: marginal utility per franc, shown per 100 FCFA** ($MU \times 100 / P$).

| Unit | $MU$ ice cream | $MU/P$ ice cream (per 100 FCFA) | $MU$ cake | $MU/P$ cake (per 100 FCFA) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | 90 | 9 | 55 | 11 |
| 2nd | 60 | **6** | 50 | 10 |
| 3rd | 30 | 3 | 45 | 9 |
| 4th | 20 | 2 | 40 | 8 |
| 5th | 0 | 0 | 35 | 7 |
| 6th | $-20$ | $-2$ | 30 | **6** |

**Step 3: equal marginal utility per franc.** The ratios are equal (6 Utils per 100 FCFA) for the **2nd unit of ice cream** ($60/1\,000$) and the **6th unit of cake** ($30/500$): $\dfrac{60}{1\,000} = \dfrac{30}{500} = 0.06$.

**Step 4: check the budget.** $2 \times 1\,000 + 6 \times 500 = 2\,000 + 3\,000 = 5\,000$ FCFA, so the whole budget is spent.

**Check against other affordable combinations that exhaust the budget:**

| Ice cream | Cake | Cost (FCFA) | Total utility (Utils) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 6 | 5 000 | $150 + 255 = 405$ |
| 3 | 4 | 5 000 | $180 + 190 = 370$ |
| 4 | 2 | 5 000 | $200 + 105 = 305$ |
| 5 | 0 | 5 000 | $200 + 0 = 200$ |

(Combinations with more than 6 cakes are beyond the table.)

**Conclusion.** The consumer is in equilibrium when he buys **2 units of ice cream and 6 units of cake**. This gives the highest total utility, **405 Utils**, and uses the entire budget of 5 000 FCFA.

questions.enonce_markdown: List two factors that can cause the budget line to change. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The budget line shows all combinations of two goods that a consumer can buy with a given income at given prices. It changes (shifts or pivots) because of (any two, 1 mark each):

1. **A change in the consumer's income.** A rise in income shifts the budget line outwards, parallel to the original line; a fall in income shifts it inwards.
2. **A change in the price of one of the goods** (or of both). A fall in the price of a good makes the line pivot outwards on the axis of that good, and a rise makes it pivot inwards. If both prices change in the same proportion, the line shifts in parallel.

questions.enonce_markdown: List two characteristics of indifference curves. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
An indifference curve joins all the combinations of two goods that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction. Its characteristics (any two, 2 marks each: statement and explanation):

1. **It slopes downwards from left to right (negative slope).** To keep satisfaction unchanged, if the consumer takes more of one good he must give up some of the other.
2. **It is convex to the origin.** The marginal rate of substitution (the amount of one good given up for one more unit of the other) falls as the consumer moves down the curve, because of diminishing marginal utility.
3. **Two indifference curves never intersect.** If they did, one combination would give two different levels of satisfaction, which contradicts consistent (transitive) preferences.
4. **A higher indifference curve (further from the origin) represents a higher level of satisfaction**, because it contains combinations with more of at least one good.
